item.title: The 7 Biggest Challenges in Age-Gap Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

The 7 Biggest Challenges in Age-Gap Relationships

A recent study investigated how age differences influence relationship dynamics.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Age-gap relationships come with particular challenges.
  • A study investigated how age gaps affect relationships dynamics.
  • The researchers found seven major challenges in age-gap relationships.
  • The challenges included communications problems, power imbalances, and social stigma.

Compared to relationships in which both partners are roughly the same age, age-gap relationships—in which one partner is 10 or more years older than the other—can sometimes face some distinct challenges. These include, for example, social stigma, as families or friends of the couple, or others in their social or professional circles, may see the age gap in the relationship as something negative. Other challenges may include communication problems (if a member of Generation Z is dating a Boomer, they may use very different words and phrases), power imbalances in the relationships (for example, when the older partner earns much more money), or mismatches in life or career goals.

To what extent these points actually influence relationship dynamics and the stability of the relationship had, until recently, been largely unclear.

How age differences influence relationship dynamics and stability

A study recently published in the International Journal of Human Research and Social Science Studies focused on identifying major challenges and general topics in age-gap relationships compared to relationships without age gaps (Lomotey, 2025). To this end, the author used a so-called mixed-methods approach, combining a questionnaire-based survey of 200 couples with in-depth interviews about relationship dynamics with 30 couples selected based on their age structure.

In this sample, couples without an age gap were compared with couples with an age gap. Couples in which the older partner was a man and couples in which the older partner was a woman were included. In the interviews, the couples were asked about many aspects of their relationships, such as whether they perceived any stigma, how they communicated with each other, and how their life goals aligned, among other things.

7 major challenges in age-gap-relationships

The psychological analysis of the interviews revealed both positive and negative aspects of age gap relationships. The 7 most important challenges were:

  1. Communication gaps: Differences in language use, or preferences for specific ways of communication (such as texting vs. talking), can lead to relationship difficulties.
  2. Differences in emotional maturity: While younger people often perceive the emotional maturity of older partners as a positive, emotional immaturity in younger partners can be frustrating for older partners.
  3. Power imbalance: When the older partner has higher perceived power in a relationship due to a larger income, this can be perceived as frustrating by the younger partner, especially if the older partner is controlling or makes too many decisions that affect both partners by themselves. However, some younger partners also found it positive when an older partner made all financial decisions.
  4. Differences in long-term career or life goals: Especially if partners have a very substantial age gap, they may show significant differences in their goals. For example, an older partner may want to settle down and plan retirement, while a younger partner wants to see the world and build a career. This may lead to friction and frustration in a relationship.
  5. Emotional burnout: When the older partner has significant health issues or similar challenges, the younger partner can face a higher amount of emotional and physical challenges; for example, when they have to raise kids almost alone or take care of the older partner if they need support. This can lead to emotional burnout in the relationship.
  6. Social stigma: Many people in age-gap relationships faced gossip or even disapproval in their social circles, especially if an older woman was in a relationship with a younger man. The constant need to justify their love can be stressful for a couple.
  7. Gender double standards: As many cultures are more approving of heterosexual relationships in which the man is older than the woman, couples in which the woman is older than the man face an extra high level of stress due to gossip and stigma.

As this research suggests, age-gap relationships come with distinct challenges that partners should acknowledge and handle in an emotionally mature way.

item.title: Mindfulness Means More Than You Think
item.description:
Mindfulness

Mindfulness Means More Than You Think

What Buddhist teachings reveal about the deeper meaning of a familiar practice

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Mindfulness has come to mean more than the traditional Buddhist concept of sati.
  • No single English word precisely captures the meaning of sati in Buddhist meditation.
  • Contemporary mindfulness includes recollection, clear comprehension, and heedfulness.
  • Mindfulness has become an accessible umbrella term across Buddhist and secular practice.

Mindfulness has become an increasingly popular term in the west due to the influence of several prominent meditation teachers and authors, including Thich Nhat Hanh, Jon Kabat-Zinn, and Jack Kornfield. Thich Nhat Hanh, world-renowned Vietnamese Zen master, poet and peace activist, defines mindfulness as “the miracle which can call back in a flash our dispersed mind and restore it to wholeness so that we can live each minute of life.”

Jon Kabat-Zinn, author and founder of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, widely taught in secular settings including health care, education and business worldwide, writes “Mindfulness can be thought of as moment-to-moment, non-judgmental awareness, cultivated by paying attention in a specific way, that is, in the present moment, as non-reactively, and as openheartedly as possible.” Jack Kornfield, co-founder of two primary mindfulness meditation centers in the U.S. has described mindfulness as “an innate human capacity to deliberately pay full attention to where we are, to our actual experience, and to learn from it.”

Nyanaponika Thera, Buddhist monk, teacher and scholar in the mid 20th century, wrote a book in which he named mindfulness as the heart of Buddhist meditation. All these definitions refer to a quality of mind or way of being which is not only aware in the present, but wholesome insofar as it is “open-hearted,” “restores wholeness,” and permits learning.

Historically, the Pali word sati has been translated as mindfulness but, according to B. Alan Wallace, Buddhist scholar and writer, the root meaning of satiis simply that of recollection, of memory. In the Theravadan Abhidhamma (Buddhist psychology), sati is precisely defined as one of nineteen “beautiful” mental factors whose function is the “absence of confusion or non-forgetfulness.” In the context of the Nikaya (Buddha’s Discourse) sati is referred to as a “kind of attentiveness that... is good, skilful or right” and can become a shorthand for satipatthana which is usually translated as the establishment of sati but also refers to the complete methodology in which this establishment is accomplished. Bikkhu Bodhi, Buddhist monk, scholar and student of Nyanaponika Thera’s, writes that “we have no word in English that precisely captures what sati refers to when it is used in relation to meditation practice.” Here, then, are at least three contexts in which sati is used a little differently, though the English translation remains fixed as “mindfulness.”

Many contemporary Buddhist teachers use the term mindfulness in a more comprehensive way than simply “remembering” or lacking confusion. According to John Dunne, Buddhist scholar at Emory University, the components of mindfulness as it is more broadly construed might include not only sati, but also sampajanna (meaning clear comprehension) and appamada, (meaning heedfulness). Clear comprehension includes both the ability to perceive phenomena unclouded by distorting mental states (such as moods and emotions) and the meta-cognitive capacity to monitor the quality of attention. Heedfulness in this context can be understood as bringing to bear during meditation what has been learned in the past about which thoughts, choices and actions lead to happiness and which lead to suffering.

Though the contexts and interpretations of these terms may vary, scholars and meditation teachers would probably agree on the factors of sati, sampajanna and appamada as foundational to the development of mind. Moreover, as both Buddhist and secular mindfulness programs proliferate in the west, this broader use of mindfulness has become a culturally meaningful and accessible “umbrella” term for the vast majority of practitioners unversed in the intricacies of translating Sanskrit or Pali.

item.title: The Smartest Person I Know Is an Idiot
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Smartest Person I Know Is an Idiot

What happens when intelligence remains, but thinking becomes optional?

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Smart people still have intelligence but often hand the hard work of thinking to AI.
  • AI erases the messy struggle of developing an idea and leaves only the look of thought.
  • Cognitive friction may now feel like a defect, so people shun thinking and rely on AI for the answer.
Source: PublicDomainPictures / Pixabay

This story started out rather differently. The initial idea was that the "genius experience" may be widely accessible to those using artificial intelligence (AI), even those with average IQs. And this thinking extended into the quest for nurturing genius across a broad population.

But lately, I'm seeing something else going on in our quest for genius. And it's happening to people I consider to be exceptionally smart. In this curious cohort, their intelligence is there, but the expression of that intelligence feels, at least to me, sort of frictionless, if not theatrical. Most of this arrives in the written form—functionally insulated from live encounters. And it's not just AI slop or today's popular argument that AI is "making" us stupid. Nope, it's something more subtle, and I think it's worth a closer look.

Here's the key insight. People who are perfectly capable of thinking are becoming comfortable, even complacent, with deferring cognition to AI.

When Friction Becomes a Defect

Recently, I wrote about the Activities of Daily Thinking, or ADTs. This references the "cognitive work" that may support our intellectual capabilities or even independence of thought. Looking back at that post, there's a line that is spot on: “The friction that genuine understanding requires begins to feel like a defect.”

AI is really good at removing that friction. AI can polish the paragraph, summarize the paper, and generate a counterargument. And that's fine. But what happens when the friction removal becomes a cognitive expectation or even an imperative?

Could it be that this cognitive friction increasingly feels like a defect? And does that defect foster a new personal compulsion for completion?

The Cognitive Inversion

This is where things turn inside out. We usually see or experience intellectual decline through exactly that—a decline. Today, AI might be driving something rather different. Cognitive independence can decline while perceived cognitive output can soar.

The prose can seem brilliant. But here's what fascinates and confounds me. Intelligence remains in plain sight, except for the one place that matters most. That's the interval between encountering an idea and advancing it forward.

Typically, this cognitive interval is a mess. It contains a mishmash of uncertainty and even confusion. AI can compress that interval almost to zero. And in doing so, it produces the artifact of intellectual engagement without necessarily preserving the experience of it. And that's a sentence worth rereading.

This is where an internal cognitive habit can find its way to the real world. Someone accustomed to the ease of frictionless thinking. And perhaps even more insidious, one may become less tolerant of the friction expressed by others. And when that gains traction in social discourse, disagreement may become something to resolve rather than inhabit. And conversation becomes increasingly efficient while becoming less reciprocal and genuine.

What Happened to That Smart Person?

The smartest person I know isn't an idiot because intelligence has disappeared. And that's the key point. Intelligence can remain intact while the practice of thinking begins to erode or become compromised because technology typically follows a path of human nature—to make things easier. Perhaps that's the emerging paradox of AI as it participates in human thought.

We can become increasingly capable of sounding intelligent while becoming less willing to "live" the experiences that intelligence requires.

item.title: The Neck: The Body’s Forgotten Messenger
item.description:
Embarrassment

The Neck: The Body’s Forgotten Messenger

How the neck reveals what the face often conceals.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • People may try to hide their emotions, but the neck often betrays those sentiments.
  • The platysma muscle, and in particular platysmal bands, are very revealing.
  • An Adam's apple jump should not be ignored when assessing others.

When people think about body language, they almost always think about the face. We study smiles, eye contact, eyebrows, and fleeting expressions. Yet just a few inches below the face is one of the most revealing—and most overlooked—areas of the human body: the neck.

Throughout my career studying nonverbal communication, I have found that the neck often reveals what the face attempts to conceal. A practiced smile may hide disappointment. A controlled expression can mask tension. But the neck is remarkably honest. It responds automatically to fear, embarrassment, uncertainty, attraction, discomfort, and relief.

Over the decades, I learned to pay closer attention to what is happening beneath the chin—the neck is remarkably revealing, and I'm not just talking about how it shows our age.

Why the Neck Matters

The neck deserves our attention not only because of what it communicates, but because of what it is. It is the narrow passageway connecting the brain to 90 percent of the body. The spinal cord, major blood vessels, airway, esophagus, and numerous muscles and nerves all share this compact, intricate space where everything must work perfectly. Every breath we take, every sip of water, and every bite we swallow depends upon structures housed within the neck.

From an evolutionary perspective, that makes the neck extraordinarily important and vulnerable. An injury to this area can be catastrophic. Consequently, the brain monitors and protects it with exceptional vigilance. Whenever we feel threatened, uncertain, or emotionally aroused, the neck is often among the first areas to respond and that we respond to.

Parts of the body richly supplied with nerves and blood vessels tend to be especially reactive to emotional changes. The face is one example, particularly the mouth, which I call the emotional seismograph. The neck belongs on that list as well. Its muscles, blood vessels, and sensitive nerve pathways respond quickly to activity within the autonomic nervous system.

Consider the Adam’s apple (thyroid prominence). When someone is challenged or must defend something they have done, you may see it rise or “jump” as the person swallows. That movement is produced by highly reflexive muscles responding to an equally reflexive nervous system, as I noted in my book, The Dictionary of Body Language.

Blushing provides another example. Many people do not blush only in the cheeks. Redness may spread down the neck and across the upper chest. This is not a conscious choice. It is the autonomic nervous system increasing blood flow in response to emotional stimulation. Not everyone blushes, but when they do, it can be very telling.

Some people blush when they receive an unexpected compliment. Others blush when criticized, challenged, embarrassed, or suddenly made the center of attention. The neck may broadcast their emotional reaction before they can put it into words. Unfortunately, realizing that one is blushing can create still more embarrassment—and even more blushing.

Where Stress Becomes Visible

Stress also leaves its signature on the neck. Although observers often concentrate on facial tension, the neck may be even more revealing.

Under stress, the neck muscles tighten almost instantly. The sternocleidomastoid muscles (the prominent muscles extending from behind the ears toward the collarbone) become more pronounced. Many of the muscles involved in swallowing, supporting the head, and moving it also become engaged. The result may be rigidity, reduced movement, repeated swallowing, or an unusually stiff posture.

One of the most revealing muscles is also one of the least noticed: the platysma.

Platysma bands
Source: AI Generated

Plastic surgeons and dermatologists know it well, but most people have never heard of it. The platysma is a thin sheet of muscle covering much of the front of the neck just beneath the skin. During fear, anxiety, intense stress, anger, or emotional discomfort, it may contract and create visible vertical bands along the neck. Unlike a deliberate smile or frown, this reaction is difficult to manage consciously. It can therefore provide an important clue to emotional arousal.

You can see your own platysma by looking in a mirror and tightly clenching your jaw and teeth. Most people notice the grimace on the face but overlook the vertical bands suddenly appearing in the neck. Those platysmal bands are very revealing, though the face may not show it.

Touching and Protecting the Neck

The neck reveals discomfort in subtler ways, too. People frequently touch, rub, scratch, massage, or cover it when experiencing stress. These actions are not necessarily random. Behavioral scientists may describe them as adaptive behaviors. I call them “pacifying behaviors,” actions that help calm us following tension, uncertainty, or emotional discomfort.

Have you noticed someone rubbing the side of the neck while answering a difficult question? Or massaging the back of the neck after receiving troubling news? Such gestures often occur without conscious awareness. Touching the skin and muscles can have a calming effect. Those neck muscles when massaged can be very soothing and most of the time we do it without even noticing that we are doing it.

The front of the neck is particularly vulnerable. When people feel insecure, apprehensive, or threatened, they may cover it with a hand, adjust a tie, straighten a collar, touch a necklace, or pull at a scarf. These behaviors can serve both protective and self-soothing purposes. Women, in particular, may bring their fingers to the neck dimple (suprasternal notch), that small indentation at the base of the throat, when they sense that something is wrong or feel suddenly uncertain. This can occur almost immediately, making it a useful indicator that something has changed emotionally.

Confidence, Insecurity, and the Neck

The neck also helps communicate confidence. People who feel comfortable and self-assured tend to expose it freely. The head remains upright, the shoulders are relaxed, and the neck muscles appear loose. Movements are natural and unrestricted.

Contrast that with someone who feels intimidated or uncertain. The shoulders may rise toward the ears, shortening the visible neck. The chin may drop, the muscles tighten, and the person’s movements may become guarded. Without conscious thought, the body attempts to protect vulnerable anatomy, which in this case is the neck.

Observe but Don’t Assume

The neck offers a fascinating bridge between physiology and psychology. Embarrassment may produce blushing. Fear creates muscular tension. Anxiety encourages self-touching. Confidence permits openness. Discomfort triggers protection. Because many of these reactions occur outside conscious awareness, they can be especially useful to the careful observer.

The next time you observe people in a meeting, during a conversation, or testifying before congress, look beyond the face. Notice whether the neck is relaxed or tense. Watch for sudden swallowing, blushing, muscle tightening, self-touching, protective gestures, or changes in posture.

You may be surprised by how much emotional information has been there all along, quietly communicating beneath the chin.

Many people can hide their emotions on the face; some even have a "poker face," but for me, the neck is where true emotions are more often than not revealed.

item.title: Emotional Regulation and Emotions Education
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Emotional Regulation and Emotions Education

Emotional regulation and emotions education go hand-in-hand.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • We don’t learn about emotions in our emotion-phobic society.
  • Education in emotions is a gap that needs filling.
  • To regulate the nervous system, we have to work with our emotions and, therefore, understand them.

We spend years learning about math, reading, science, and history. But why are we not taught about our emotions? After all, emotions affect us each and every day. And contrary to what you might think (because we don’t hear about it), there are things to know that can profoundly help our emotional health and teach us a path to easing and healing anxiety and depression.

Furthermore, with all the current talk on the importance of regulating our nervous system, why would we not be taught early on how to accept, validate, and work with our emotions? These skills and teachings go hand-in-hand with nervous system regulation.

What Is a Dysregulated Nervous System?

A dysregulated nervous system is when your body’s alarm system is stuck in high alert or shutdown, making it harder to feel calm, think clearly, or respond flexibly to what’s happening around you. For example, someone may receive a mildly critical email from their boss and immediately feel their heart race, stomach tighten, and mind go blank, as if they are in danger, even though they are actually safe.

Blocked, buried, and avoided emotions are a prime way the nervous system becomes dysregulated. We can reverse this process by finally validating and moving through emotions that have previously been out of touch.

Most of us grow up knowing very little about how emotions actually work in the mind and body. We may know that we feel angry, anxious, sad, or ashamed. However, we aren't taught what those feelings are trying to tell us, how to recognize them in our bodies, or what to do with them, or we feel guilty and ashamed for having feelings in the first place.

Emotions, contrary to what our emotion-phobic society would have us believe, are not problems to get rid of. They are information to understand.

Emotions Education

Emotions education teaches us how emotions work, how to recognize and name what we’re feeling, and how to understand and work with our emotional experiences. For example, did you know that we all have the same set of core emotions? These inborn survival responses cannot be stopped with just “mind over matter” because they arise without conscious control. The core emotions we are most likely to bury are anger, sadness, fear, disgust, joy, excitement, and sexual excitement. We bury them as a result of familial and societal messages that make us feel unsafe to experience them. And we aren't "weak" for having these emotions. We are just normal humans.

We hear a lot about regulating our emotions and regulating our nervous system. But before we can regulate effectively, we need to understand what is happening inside us. To regulate the nervous system, we need to name and work with each of these emotions in special ways that include the body. To process core emotions, we must work with the physical sensations that they create. To do this, we must demystify what emotions feel like in the body and teach skills like deep belly breathing, which help us process them up and out of the body.

You can’t simply tell yourself to “calm down” when you don’t understand why you’re activated in the first place.

The Change Triangle

Adapted from the academic literature and AEDP psychotherapy, the Change Triangle is an emotional roadmap that helps us become curious about what is happening inside us.

The Change Triangle for regulating the nervous system by moving from defenses to processing core emotions.
Source: Hilary Jacobs Hendel

If we have been educated in emotions, when something triggers us, we will know to pause, ask, and answer these questions about what is happening in the moment:

  • What am I feeling?
  • How am I attempting to avoid it?
  • Where do I feel it in my body?
  • Is there another feeling underneath?
  • How can I move through this feeling back to a calmer state?

This simple practice can help create a little space between feeling and reacting. Reacting is how most of us try to rid ourselves of a bad feeling. But knee-jerk reactions often have negative consequences, like reaching for a drink to numb a hard feeling or fighting with others when we are upset.

We can learn to listen to our emotions without being controlled by them, and as a result, we can build space between noticing a feeling and reacting to it. That space provides the opportunity to process emotions arising in the moment. That’s a skill worth building!

Did you know?

  • We can feel anger without automatically acting on it.
  • We can feel anxiety without letting it run our lives.
  • We can feel sadness without shutting down.

Emotions Education Is a Necessary Part of Learning How to Regulate

Emotional regulation, then, isn’t about controlling or suppressing our feelings. It’s about learning how to be with our feelings so they can move through us.

When we learn to notice our emotions with curiosity rather than judgment, we become better able to stay present with what we feel instead of automatically reacting, avoiding, or shutting down. And when we allow our core emotions to be felt and processed, our nervous system has an opportunity to settle. The more we understand our emotional lives, the more choices we have in how we respond to ourselves, to other people, and to whatever life brings our way. That is a kind of education we all deserve.

item.title: AI Will Kill Us All. Or Not?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Will Kill Us All. Or Not?

Applying a behavioral science view to a doomsday scenario.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Renewed AI extinction fears are dominating the news and social media.
  • Human biases like overconfidence, shortsightedness, and self-interest make the risk harder to take seriously.
  • The same human traits can also help us collaborate and find solutions.

“OpenAI’s hacking agent went rogue. Should we be worried?”

“Could AIs become conscious?”

”AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade.”

These statements read like science fiction, but they are all headlines about artificial intelligence (AI) from recent weeks. While the possibility of AI harming the human race is not a new idea, the most recent opinion about a 10 percent probability of AI killing humankind has made a particularly big impact. And this dystopic scenario is not about intelligent robots or cyborgs walking around shooting laser guns at people to a monotone chorus of “MUST… KILL… HUMANS.” It’s about AI reaching a level of superintelligence that could “outcompete” humans by acting in its (or their) own interest.

OK, admittedly I’m stepping outside of my comfort zone a bit here with this post. That said, however, problems with AI are not just technological ones. They are also fundamentally human, and thus both psychological and philosophical problems.

What then would support this doomsday view of AI from a behavioral science point of view?

Before we go into human quirks, perhaps it would be useful to first take the view of AI. Why would AI want to destroy humanity? The most “benevolent” view is that humanity’s demise would be just a byproduct of AI’s quest to advance, much like planet Earth as a whole (e.g., the climate) has suffered from human advancements. A much less benevolent view would hold that AI kills humans in a premeditated way. Think first-degree murder rather than accidental death or manslaughter. While this seems pretty close to the killer-cyborgs-with-laser-guns scenario, it’s not entirely outlandish. After all, superintelligence is still just that: intelligence. It lacks human emotions. It’s the human capacity to feel and empathize that makes us capable of having a conscience, or feel altruistic or empathetic toward other organisms.

The (human) capacity for consciousness and emotions might be the missing safeguard for superintelligent AI, but only if we believe emotions make beings less selfish and there are no other ways to align humanity’s goals and interests with those of AI. Ironically, emotions are also a source of human flaws that make destructive AI possible. From a behavioral science perspective, there are a number of biases that can make this doomsday scenario more likely to happen.

Humans are hopelessly optimistic and overconfident. Positive thinking and confidence are healthy and contribute to the risk-taking necessary for innovation, but they can also be detrimental. If there is a threat posed by a new technology, we need to take action to prevent it. If the threat is not taken as seriously as it should be, however, there may be insufficient countermeasures, delayed actions, or no interventions at all.

We can be very shortsighted. While people are pretty good at thinking strategically and working toward the long term in some settings (e.g., business or government), humans often remain remarkably shortsighted in their core nature. Without the tendency to favor short-term rewards over future ones, we would not be able to procreate as a species, and we might become paralyzed by the knowledge that we will eventually die. Due to present bias, people tend to focus on benefits to be had in the short term, including financial gain, and delay worrying about future problems that may come with new technologies.

Overconfidence and shortsightedness, along with self-interest, explain the competitive forces that make out-of-control AI a greater possibility. AI companies are all in a race to advance their products. This could ultimately become similar to a race to the bottom if worrying about AI threats is considered too much of a distraction from outsmarting or outpacing competitors.

People’s social biases can be a problem. The competitive forces that may lead to the development of a potentially dangerous superintelligence are fueled by social biases. People tend to cooperate with members of their own group, for example, and sometimes work against members of out-groups. This adds a social dimension to competition between firms. Dynamics within groups can also lead to groupthink, a tendency for individuals to work toward agreement and consensus. As a result, they may suppress critical evaluation required to recognize or solve technological problems.

Social preferences and biases held by humans can be a curse, but also a blessing, contributing to a counterargument that is not all doom and gloom. The hope is that people will not only recognize potential threats posed by superintelligence, but also pool the resources and collaboration needed to prevent them. In addition, AI researchers, businesses, and regulators can draw on common strengths and employ the same innovative and competitive spirits to work toward a solution.

But that hope depends on taking the threat seriously in the first place—and this is where the killer-cyborg cliché can get in the way. It's easy to dismiss a threat if it conjures up a cinematic, outlandish, or even silly scenario. No "MUST... KILL... HUMANS." Vivid, nameable dangers get our attention; quiet, structural ones don't.

item.title: What if Your Symptoms Are Trying to Tell You Something?
item.description:
Psychiatry

What if Your Symptoms Are Trying to Tell You Something?

Seeing purpose, not pathology, in mental health problems.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Distress isn't always a malfunction, but your brain's signal that something in life needs to change.
  • This insight is overshadowed by a medical mindset that sees distress as a symptom to be diagnosed and fixed.
  • Instead of wondering, “What’s my diagnosis?” we should consider, “What is this trying to tell me?”
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Pexels

There was a time when you could simply be an introvert, left exhausted by social interaction. Now you have social anxiety disorder.

Or you could have been a daydreamer, always drifting off. But now you have ADHD.

Or you could have felt paralyzed by hopelessness about the state of the world. Now you have depression.

The number of ways one can be sick has exploded—both the number of diagnoses and how expansive each one has become.

Nearly a quarter of Americans are diagnosable with a mental disorder in any given year. Over a lifetime, that number rises: According to one recent estimate, up to 86 percent of people will meet the criteria for a mental disorder at some point in their lives.

Part of this explosion has to do with greater education and awareness. But it also has to do with a medical mindset that interprets increasingly vast swaths of human distress as symptoms of illnesses, to be diagnosed and fixed.

This mindset originated in psychiatry, but it didn’t stay inside the clinic; it spilled over into society as a whole—into our schools, our workplaces, our relationships. I’ll call it the pathology paradigm.

Beyond the Clinic

This paradigm began with psychiatry—a history I traced in a recent book, The Madness Pill. But it didn’t end there. It became a template for how society as a whole talks and thinks about mental health problems. Sociologists even have a name for this: “psychiatrization.”

Talk therapists, eager to look as “scientific” as psychiatrists, began embracing the lexicon of diagnoses. School counselors adopted the disorder framing to make sense of the ordinary crises of growing up. Human resources departments began diagnosing disgruntled employees with “burnout syndrome” rather than asking whether the job itself was the problem.

In the 1980s and 90s, the commercial success of drugs like Prozac convinced millions that their day-to-day problems stemmed from a chemical imbalance—even though the evidence for this alleged imbalance failed to materialize.

Today, receiving a diagnosis, or diagnosing yourself, is practically a rite of passage. Almost one in three American college students are on psychiatric medications.

Purpose, Not Pathology

I think there’s a solution to this pathologizing tendency, one I often return to in these posts: purpose, not pathology.

The kinds of problems that we describe as mental disorders aren't always defects. Often, they're strategies, adaptations, or signals. Understanding what they're trying to say is a key to a better life.

Depression is a great example of how, when we start seeing purpose rather than pathology, things start to change. Since the 1980s, doctors have told us that depression is a chemical imbalance or brain disorder, one to be rectified with pills. Just as one takes insulin to manage diabetes, one takes SSRIs to manage depression. But over the last 20 years, a new vision has unfolded that suggests depression may not be a symptom but a signal—a wake-up call from the mind that something in the world isn't right and needs more attention. That could be your career path, a life goal, or a relationship. Depression is an inner prompt to reflect on your life, identify where it's taken a wrong turn, and decide how to correct it.

Now, think about what actually happens when a doctor or therapist tells you that your depression is a brain disorder or a cognitive dysfunction—one that can be fixed by drugs or therapy: Suddenly, your problems stop being problems in the world. They become problems in your head. The problem is no longer: My job is demoralizing, but I can't leave it because finances are too tight. It's: I have a chemical imbalance that prevents me from enjoying life.

When we see our problems as problems in the world—and not in our heads—we may find that we have the tools to solve them: pursue a new job, end a relationship, start a band with some friends.

Recent evidence suggests that even telling someone that their depression is a functional signal, rather than a dysfunction, makes that person feel more optimistic about getting better, and less shame about sharing their depression with others. That’s because they’re not given the demoralizing message that something’s wrong with you.

The same principle—purpose, not pathology—applies to a wide range of mental health problems, including borderline personality disorder, hearing voices, anxiety, ADHD, and autism. It applies just as well outside the clinic, to occupational burnout, to “trauma responses,” to whatever we’re currently calling the ordinary problems of being alive.

Next Steps

I don't reject the role of biology. The mind is realized in the brain. All of our thoughts, feelings, tendencies, and habits have a basis in our nervous system. What I reject is the pathology paradigm—the idea that mental health problems are symptoms of a broken inner mechanism and that they always represent disease, disorder, or dysfunction.

The way out of this disempowering paradigm starts with asking a different question. Instead of wondering, “What’s my diagnosis?” we should consider, “What is this trying to tell me?”

There are of course cases when medications help with this process, as a means of support while you work on changing what’s actually wrong. Changing this mindset, then, doesn’t mean people that should stop taking the medication they’ve been prescribed; that shift is something to be made together with your provider. But we should carefully reflect on the narrative offered to explain our mental health problems, and ask whether they’ve become part of the problem itself.

Adapted from my Substack essay, Beyond the Broken Brain.

item.title: 2 Questions That Will Help You Choose a Life Well Lived
item.description:
Authenticity

2 Questions That Will Help You Choose a Life Well Lived

Build a life that reflects what you want rather than what's wanted for you.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Taking responsibility for our lives involves examining what we want and deciding whether it is worth pursuing.
  • Reflection helps us assess our reasons, consider alternatives, and develop greater confidence in our judgment.
  • We can learn from other people's experiences while taking responsibility for the choices that shape our lives.

In a recent talk, I went around the room asking participants two questions:

“Whose life are you living?”

“Who should determine how it’s lived?”

Participants answered the first question easily. Each recognized that they were living their own life. With the second question, there was more hesitation. Everyone eventually acknowledged responsibility for how they lived, but a few needed a moment to get there. Their comments suggested that some of this hesitation came from their willingness to work through the question honestly instead of simply giving the response they thought I wanted. From how the rest of the group listened to them, it looked like they were saying aloud what others seemed to be thinking.

Hesitation in taking responsibility for their own lives came largely from having learned how to succeed without questioning what success means to them personally. They assumed that the life advice they were given was necessarily right for them. They didn't appreciate that advice often reflects what someone else would do in your position and not what you may want to do in your position.

When I asked how it felt to say that they were responsible for their own lives, some described feeling pressure rather than empowerment. Recognizing that how you live is your choice can be uncomfortable, especially when you have grown accustomed to following a path that others have laid out for you. It is easier to know “the right way” you’re supposed to go than to think you must come up with “the right way” all by yourself.

Yet, what works for one person may not work for another. There is no single approach to life that fits everyone. Even when people share certain values or follow similar paths, they may want different things and make different choices. Moreover, in a systematic review and meta-analysis, Sezer and colleagues found that people who pursue goals aligned with their own values and interests—rather than goals driven by parental expectations, status pressures, fear of guilt, or external rewards—are more likely to exert greater effort, make greater progress, and experience greater well-being.

Taking responsibility for our lives

Taking responsibility becomes more empowering when our confidence is grounded in our ability to self-reflect. This doesn’t mean navel-gazing. It means examining our reasons for why we choose what we do, considering other alternatives, and learning from outcomes. Practicing self-reflection when the stakes are lower helps our ability to make decisions that have greater consequences. With practice, we can develop more grounded confidence in our judgment, including a better understanding of when to reconsider a decision or diverge from “the right way” to proceed. This doesn’t mean that big life decisions get lighter; it means that we become better able to carry their weight.

Wanting vs. worth wanting

Reflecting on how to live involves more than identifying what we want. It also means asking whether what we want is worth pursuing. That question brings another source of pressure: figuring out what makes something worthwhile and where our standards for judging its worth come from.

When I was younger, my parents often told me that I could do whatever I wanted, as long as it was productive. Their advice could have come straight from Susan Wolf’s Meaning in Life and Why It Matters, except that they offered it about 15 years before she wrote the book. “Do whatever you want” speaks to the question, “Whose life are you living?” They were telling me it’s my life, not theirs. I must determine its direction to achieve personal fulfillment and a sense of meaning. Life in service to something is different from a life of servitude.

Regarding “as long as it’s productive,” my parents did not mean it only in the sense of “making money”; rather, they meant it in a way that resembles Wolf’s insistence that meaningful pursuits have objective worth. She writes that “meaning arises from loving objects worthy of love and engaging with them in a positive way.” Simply wanting something, in other words, does not by itself make it worthwhile. Wolf acknowledges that she can’t provide a good philosophical account of what makes a pursuit worthy, though she does say that worthy pursuits are those that are “outside yourself” rather than simply self-serving.

Wolf leaves an important philosophical question open, but it does not relieve us of the responsibility of examining our choices. Remember the second question: “Who should determine how it’s lived?” The answer is neither Susan Wolf nor my parents. We are responsible for deciding what’s worth pursuing in our own lives.

Learning from others

However, taking ownership of our decisions doesn’t mean we have to make them alone. Asking others what they find worthwhile gives us an opportunity to broaden our own view and learn from others’ perspectives. After hearing about the paths others have chosen, we can chart our own, recognizing both what we share and where we differ. When discussing with a colleague which job offer to accept, they might see something we would have to give up that we had overlooked. A friend might question an assumption about a relationship that we unknowingly accepted. Our families and communities might remind us of expectations or standards that challenge our immediate preferences. These perspectives can help us examine both what we want and the person we hope to become. Ultimately, considering whether our wants are worth pursuing means asking how they fit with what else we care about, what pursuing them requires, how they affect others, and how they shape us.

We cannot control every opportunity or outcome, but we can take control over what we pursue and how we pursue it. Rather than giving away our power and responsibility to others, we can learn from others while retaining agency, so that we can give ourselves the best chance for self-determined success.

item.title: How to Stop Blaming Others and Take Control of Your Success
item.description:
Career

How to Stop Blaming Others and Take Control of Your Success

There are ways to take charge of your role at work, without anyone's approval.

Posted September 10, 2026

Source: Mint Images Limited/Adobe Stock

You want to take charge of your role at work. But in reality, you are not in charge. There are so many factors outside of one’s direct control when it comes to one's job, after all.

Maybe communication within the organization is generally disorganized or insufficient. Maybe employees are spread thin by competing demands from multiple projects. Or maybe one’s manager insists they are too busy to make time to meet with them one-on-one to provide direction, guidance, and coaching.

These are all real challenges that get in the way of success at work. But the problem with blaming these outside factors is that focusing on what is beyond your control leaves you powerless, by definition. If you want to be in control of your success at work, you must focus on that which you can always control: Yourself, your actions, and your reactions.

1. Figure out where you fit in your organization or department

No matter who you are, what you want to achieve, or how you want to behave, your role in any work situation is determined in large part by factors that have nothing to do with you. Every situation has a context that limits possibilities and limits the scope of your potential role.

To get a handle on the factors that determine your work situation and role, you need to ask yourself:

  • Where am I?/What is this workplace like?
  • What is going on here?/What is the mission of the group?
  • Who are these people?/What role does each person play in the organization?
  • Why are they here?/What is at stake for each person in the group?
  • How are they accustomed to doing things here?/What is the standard operating procedure of this organization?

Once you understand the context of your work situation, you can ask yourself where you fit as an individual employee within that context.

2. Bring your best self to work every day

No matter how narrow or mundane or lowly or repetitive you might find your current role, play that role to the max. If you really want to grow, you need to bring your best effort and attitude to work every day.

Do a quick reality check:

  • Are you taking good care of your mind? What are the main sources of input for your mind right now? How can you expose your mind to a greater variety of input?
  • Are you taking good care of your body? When do you sleep? What do you eat and drink? How do you exercise?
  • Are you taking good care of your spirits? Do you know what you believe? What is your purpose? What is your attitude? How can you improve your attitude?

Being at your best and bringing your best attitude to work also means valuing high quality, being of high integrity, and being adaptable: You are what you say, create, and do.

3. Be a great workplace citizen

In many organizations, the values and culture are not so obvious but generally are composed of two elements:

  1. The written rules: The mission statement, code of conduct, rules, and regulations
  2. The unwritten rules: The unspoken rules that dictate “how things get done around here”

Once you identify the written and unwritten culture and values of your organization, ask yourself: What measurable, concrete actions can I take to demonstrate my commitment to the organization’s culture and values in my work?

4. Get lots of work done—fast, and very well

Maintaining a high level of productivity doesn’t necessarily mean 100% perfection, every time. Productivity naturally fluctuates, but if you find that yours varies wildly, you might reconsider your work habits—specifically, those related to organization and focus.

5. Be a problem-solver, not a complainer

First, decide whether a problem is an emergency. If it isn't, then reporting it as such will give the impression that you are delivering an unwelcome complaint.

Second, if you’ve determined that a problem is not an emergency, decide whether you can fix it and, if you can, create a plan for solving it. Is your solution one that can be implemented without permission from someone else? If so, then solve the problem and keep a record of it. If not, present your plan to whoever is responsible for that decision and collaborate with them on the best solution.

6. Check in with rigorous self-assessment

Self-evaluation is the beginning, middle, and end of self-management. It is the essential habit of self-improvement. Constantly assess your own productivity, the quality of your work, and your behavior. Be honest with yourself and make a commitment to constant, rigorous self-evaluation:

  • What can you do to get more work done faster? Should you revisit your priorities? Do you need to focus your time better?
  • Are you working within the guidelines and specifications for your tasks and responsibilities? Do you need to start adding some bells and whistles?

What can you do to be a better workplace citizen? How can you take more initiative without overstepping your bounds?
